1.pericope_label: Elihu asks Job to hear his speeches, professes that his words come from an upright heart and that the Spirit of God has made him, invites Job to answer, and offers himself in God stead as one also formed out of the clay whose terror shall not make Job afraid

schools.summary: Gill observes that the preceding chapter was addressed to the three friends and this to Job himself, and that none of the friends had ever used his name, the opening word carrying the reason, since Elihu has taken their part against nobody and has blamed them, and he is full of matter and uneasy until he has vented it, like new wine ready to burst; he explains that the uprightness spoken of is not the theme but the manner, these being the real sentiments of the speaker mind and not the product of a double heart, allows that men do stand in God stead and that Elihu does so here as an advocate undertaking to clear God of the charge of severity, adds the alternative rendering, I am as thou art, a frail creature accountable to God as Job is, and answers Job earlier fear from Elihu side, since a man who is neither king nor prince, and has not even age enough to command awe, has no terrible majesty to inject dread.

Henry draws out what Job is to gather from the address, that this speaker does not join the other three, having already disclaimed their method, so that where they were all in the same song he is trying a new way and asks to be heard entire, since no discourse can be judged until it is heard out, and that he means to make a solemn business of it rather than put in a word by the by to show his wit; he suspects the friends of the opposite fault, that they did not believe in their consciences the things they said of Job and said them to support a hypothesis, which he calls a base thing, to condemn with the tongue for a turn those of whom one secretly thinks well; he turns the claim of plainness into a rule, that men who speak of the things of God should avoid obscurity, since clearness shows both that they understand their subject and that they mean their hearers good; and he recalls Job own wish in his own words, that one might plead for a man with God, with the bargain attached that God dread should not make him afraid.

Clarke makes the claim of the third verse higher than the others do, that since God has given him his Spirit he will speak from that Spirit alone, laying down no false position and drawing no false consequence, and glossing the second phrase as pure knowledge; he rejects the received translation of the sixth verse altogether, since the word taken for according to thy wish is not Hebrew but Arabic with a Hebrew suffix, meaning fellow or equal, so that the line should run, Behold, I am thy fellow, I too was formed by God out of the clay; and on the last verse he makes the equality itself the point, that between equals no fear can overawe a man out of conducting his own defence; Wesley keeps the familiar reading of the sixth verse and notes that Job had often wished for just such a pleader.

Keil and Delitzsch note that no previous speaker had addressed Job by name, and make the whole discussion turn on a single condition, that Job attend to its connected contents and not to this or that piece of them; Ellicott glosses the last clause of the span simply, that he will deal gently and not be harsh.

debates.question: What does the phrase rendered according to thy wish mean?

sides.position: not Hebrew at all but Arabic with a Hebrew suffix, meaning fellow or equal: Behold, I am thy fellow
the received sense stands, Job having often wished for just such a pleader in God stead
either that or I am as thou art, a frail creature accountable to God as Job is

debates.question: Why should Job not be afraid of this speaker?

sides.position: because he is no king or prince and has not even age enough to command awe, so has no terrible majesty to inject dread
because between equals no fear can overawe a man out of conducting his own defence
because he undertakes to deal gently and not be harsh

outliers: Clarke alone throws out the received translation of the key phrase on the ground that the word is Arabic rather than Hebrew.
Keil and Delitzsch alone make the whole speech conditional on Job hearing its connected contents rather than parts of it.
themes: a speaker who names the man he addresses
plain speech promised and demanded
an umpire formed out of the same clay
a hearing asked without dread

8.pericope_label: Elihu repeats what he has heard Job say, that he is clean without transgression while God finds occasions against him and puts his feet in the stocks, and answers that in this Job is not just, for God is greater than man and gives no account of his matters

schools.summary: Gill notes that the charge rests neither on suspicion nor on report but on words heard with the speaker own ears, allows that the quoted saying is nowhere recorded in that form but thinks it did fall from Job lips during the controversy without being written down, since not everything said on either side was preserved, and is careful to say what is not denied, that Job was a just man before God and before men and lived soberly and righteously, the fault lying in this one thing, that he pressed his own innocence and attached to it undue reflections on God dealings with him.

Henry presses the public character of the charge, that it was not said in private, for then repeating it publicly would have been ill bred, but openly, and what is said openly may be openly reproved, those who sin before all being rebuked before all; he stands between the other voices on whether Job said it, granting that Job had owned himself impure before God and never claimed to be clean in so many words, yet had said that God knew he was not wicked and that he held fast his righteousness, on which the charge could be built, so that Elihu dealt unfairly in making innocence of all transgression out of a plea of innocence of the great transgression, though men who speak unwarily must thank themselves when they are misunderstood; and he makes the limited charge the difference between this speaker and the other three, who would not own Job just at all where this one says only that in saying this he is not just.

Clarke answers Job demand for reasons by denying that any are owed, God being sovereign and not to be called to the bar of his creatures, and adds that he is too wise to err and too good to be unkind; Wesley defends the charge as far as it goes, since Job meant no such transgression as would justify so severe a punishment, and distinguishes it from the accusations of the three friends, who blamed his claim to innocence because they thought him a hypocrite, where Elihu blames it because it came mixed with reflections upon God, and he widens the one proposition of the answer, that God is greater not in power and majesty only but in justice and wisdom and goodness, so that to censure his judgments is to cast off the awe a man owes his sovereign Lord.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the complaint in their own rendering, that he is pure and without transgression, spotless and without guilt, while God finds malicious things against him, counts him for an enemy, puts his feet in the stocks and observes all his paths; Ellicott denies outright that Job ever used this language, though several of his statements could be perverted into it, and holds that the misunderstanding shows that even Elihu could not enter fully into Job position, not grasping that a man is righteous in the measure that he trusts God and is then righteous with God own righteousness, which was the truth Job dimly perceived and was faintly but surely striving after, and he dissents again on the next verse, that Job had not striven against God at all but had longed to come into judgment with him, and was striving with the darkness about the throne rather than with the justice of God, which he trusted entirely.

debates.question: Did Job ever say that he was clean without transgression?

sides.position: the words are nowhere recorded, but they probably fell from him in the controversy without being written down
he never used the language; several of his statements could be perverted into it, and the misunderstanding shows Elihu could not enter fully into his position
not in so many words, but he had said enough for the charge to be built on, though the charge still overstates it
he meant no such transgression as would justify so severe a punishment, and so far the charge is just

debates.question: Is the rebuke that Job has striven against God a fair one?

sides.position: yes; he laid charges against God dealings which he could not justify, and God owes his creatures no account
yes as to this one thing, the pressing of his innocence with undue reflections on God, and no further
no; he had longed to come into judgment with God and was striving with the darkness about the throne, not with the justice of God, which he trusted

outliers: Ellicott alone turns the chapter against its own speaker, finding in the charge evidence that Elihu had not understood Job.
Wesley alone distinguishes this charge from the three friends by its motive rather than its content.
themes: a quotation Job may never have spoken
a charge narrowed to one fault
greatness as the whole of the answer
a judge who gives no account

14.pericope_label: God speaks once and twice though man perceives it not, in a dream and a vision of the night, opening the ears of men and sealing their instruction, that he may withdraw man from his purpose and hide pride from him and keep back his soul from the pit

schools.summary: Gill reads the once and twice as two methods, dreams and visions first and chastisement second, or else as simple frequency, line upon line, one way taken up when another has failed, and on the preservation that follows he takes the pit both ways, the grave where the body turns to rottenness and the bottomless pit of ruin, since the Lord people are reproved that they may not be condemned with the world.

Henry puts the exchange with Job directly, that Job had said God kept him wholly in the dark and therefore dealt with him as an enemy, where the answer is that God speaks while Job fails to perceive him, so that the fault lies on Job side and the very dispensations he puts a harsh construction on are meant for his good; it is a token of favour, he says, that the quarrel notwithstanding God should speak to us at all, and a mark of his design that he speaks to us of our own concerns, again and again, giving another warning when the first is neglected; and he explains the opening of the ear by an example, that God opens the heart as he opened Lydia and so opens the ears, which had been shut against the voice of this charmer.

Clarke takes the dream and the vision as the first two of his numbered means and defends the first against ridicule, since many have had the most salutary warnings that way, and to decry all dreams because many are vain would be about as wise as to deny the Bible because many foolish books have been written by men who thought themselves inspired, while the second he describes as images presented to the imagination in slumber, or to a man awake in bed and wrapt in contemplation, the darkness having shut out the objects that would otherwise divert the mind; he insists that the dream by itself does no good, since it is the opening of the understanding and the pouring in of light that make men wise to salvation, lists what the Spirit uses to that end, serious alarms, penitential pangs, the apprehension of death and judgment, and discoveries of justice and of love, and on the last verse keeps to the plainer sense, reckoning how many have been snatched from a sudden accident or from the knife of a murderer by taking such a warning; Wesley keeps both senses of the once and twice and lists the channels, conscience, providence and ministers, adding that God will not gratify curiosity about his hidden judgments but will acquaint a man with his duty, glosses the sealing as an imprinting of the instruction on the mind, and explains the hiding of pride by the effect of such representations of the divine majesty, which take a man off the admiration of his own excellency and show him his weakness.

Ellicott states the purpose of the whole as the main point of Elihu teaching, that the purposes of God are disciplinary, meant to keep a man from the sin he would otherwise be prone to commit, so that Job might have been a righteous man and still be justly chastened lest he prove unrighteous, and he glosses the opened ear as God showing a man the sentence he will seal up against him if he does not repent; Keil and Delitzsch read the words as describing the first mode, God coming forward as a witness in a man sleep and using dreams or dream-like visions that rise suddenly within the realm of nocturnal thought, a form of revelation especially usual in the heathen world, which lacks a positive revelation, and they note that both the manuscripts and the accents proceed from the correct assumption that a vision of the night and a dream are not the same notion.

debates.question: What are the once and the twice?

sides.position: two methods, dreams and visions first and chastisement second, or else simple frequency, line upon line
the channels of conscience, providence and ministers, with a second admonition when the first does not awaken a man
a numbered series of means, the dream and the vision being the first two of them

debates.question: What is the purpose of God speaking so?

sides.position: discipline; the purposes of God are to keep a man from the sin he would otherwise commit, so that a righteous man may be justly chastened lest he prove unrighteous
to answer Job complaint, since God does speak and the fault is in the man who does not perceive him
to keep the soul back from the pit, which is both the grave and the ruin beyond it

outliers: Clarke alone defends dreams as a channel of warning by comparing the dismissal of all dreams to the dismissal of all books.
Keil and Delitzsch alone insist that a dream and a vision of the night are two notions and not one, and read the accents as evidence of it.
themes: a God who speaks twice when once is not heard
the hour when the senses are locked up
an ear opened from within
chastening as a preservative

19.pericope_label: He is chastened also with pain upon his bed and the multitude of his bones with strong pain, so that his life abhorreth bread and his flesh is consumed away, and his soul draweth near unto the grave and his life to the destroyers

schools.summary: Gill reads the connecting word as marking another method, affliction, which has a voice in it that men of wisdom will hear, and is careful to say that the pain meant is of the body and not a wounded spirit, since it is endured on the bed where a man might have hoped for rest; on the last verse he denies that the soul strictly so called goes down to the grave, since at death it returns to God who gave it, and takes the word either of the body or of the person of the sick man, given up by physicians and friends and left at the grave mouth, which is how Job had spoken of himself.

Henry sets the whole against Job own case, that Job complained of his diseases and judged from them that God was angry, and his friends judged so too, where Elihu shows that God often afflicts the body in love with gracious designs upon the soul, which is what makes this part of the speech useful for the due improvement of sickness; he then follows the verses as a case, that the pain is not a dull heavy ache but strong and acute, turning a bed of down into a bed of thorns where the sick man tosses till the dawning of the day, an inward rooted pain in the multitude of the bones, which shows what frail bodies we have, pained from causes within themselves without any hurt from outside; on the loss of appetite he draws a lesson against daintiness, that we should not be desirous of dainties since they are deceitful meat and we may be made as sick of them as we are now fond of them; and on the wasting he observes that a few days of sickness can consume the flesh that was fat and fair until the bones that were buried in it stand out to be counted, though sickness will not make lean the soul that is fed with the bread of life.

Clarke numbers affliction as the fourth of his means and brings a witness, that it was in God hand the cause of David salvation, who said that before he was afflicted he went astray; he notes that the second clause may be rendered either of a disease in which the patient thinks every bone broken or out of joint, or of a strong multitude of bones chastened even in their vigour, and on the last verse he divides the two words, the first for the immortal spirit drawing near to corruption and the second for the animal life drawing near to those already buried, reporting a rendering of the second as the Destinies, on the view that the Hebrews had such figures as the Greeks and Latins and the northern nations had, though he thinks the plainer sense more natural; Wesley takes the destroyers for the pangs of death, just ready to seize the man.

Ellicott says shortly that this is the second manner in which God speaks, first by dreams and then by afflictions, and offers rheumatism and gout as what the second clause describes; Keil and Delitzsch use the verse to mark where the argument has got to, that the former case needed only a strengthening of the testimony of conscience by a warning given under remarkable circumstances, whereas this second case is the harder, treating not merely of a warning against sin and its wages but of a deliverance from a death already at hand.

debates.question: What does it mean that his soul draws near to the grave?

sides.position: not the soul strictly, which returns to God at death, but the body or the person, given up by physicians and left at the grave mouth
the two words divide, the immortal spirit drawing near corruption and the animal life drawing near those already buried
the pangs of death, here called the destroyers, are ready to seize him

debates.question: How is the sickness to be read?

sides.position: as a second way of speaking, alongside the dream; rheumatism and gout answer the description
as God afflicting the body in love with a gracious design on the soul, against Job inference that it proved anger
as the harder of the two cases, needing not a warning only but a deliverance from a death at hand

outliers: Clarke alone reports a rendering of the destroyers as the Destinies and sets it beside the fate-figures of the Greeks, the Latins and the north.
Henry alone turns the loss of appetite into a warning against luxury, that dainties are deceitful meat.
themes: a bed of down turned into thorns
bread loathed and flesh consumed
pain with a voice in it
a life handed over to the destroyers

23.pericope_label: If there be a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand, then he is gracious unto him and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit, I have found a ransom; his flesh shall be fresher than a child and he shall pray unto God and see his face with joy

schools.summary: Gill refuses the created angel, and though he grants that angels do attend the saints in their dying moments he adds that this proves nothing for invoking them as mediators; the messenger is rather a minister of the word, by office a messenger and an interpreter of the Scriptures, and such a man is scarce and rare. On the restoration he keeps the sense bodily and comparative, the man who had been reduced to skin and bone becoming plump again, the withered skin soft, the pale face ruddy.

Henry expands the same reading of the messenger into a rule about sickness, that when God speaks by afflictions we are often so unversed in the language that we need an interpreter, so that the help of a man who knows the voice of the rod is as needful then as a physician, and such a one is indeed one of a thousand; on the ransom he says that Christ is both the purchaser and the price, the priest and the sacrifice, that the ransom is of God own finding, a contrivance neither men nor angels could have discovered, and that God glories in the invention, repeating that he has found it.

Clarke makes the ransom the atonement, and the thing that gives all the preceding means their efficacy, since without it they would be useless and salvation impossible, and he cannot think the redemption of a lost world by Christ is obscurely signified here; he takes every clause of the restoration spiritually, that the man is born a new creature and returns to the days of his youth by becoming a child of God through faith, prayer being the very breath of that new life, and the sight of God face the knowledge that he is reconciled; Wesley makes the messenger a prophet or teacher, there to expound the providence and point out the design of God in it, notes how few are rightly qualified for so great and hard a work, keeps Henry exclamation over the ransom almost word for word and adds what the way found was, the death of the Son, with the plea that though God might justly destroy the man he will spare him, and takes both senses of the last clause of the span, the endangered life restored and the soul delivered from the pit of hell, with light standing for all good in the vision and fruition of God.

Ellicott goes furthest on the messenger, calling the office a remarkable anticipation of the function since discharged by the Advocate with the Father, and saying that one who holds all Scripture inspired cannot but see here an indication of what God meant afterwards to teach about the mediation of the Son; he fastens on the ransom from another side, that it is remarkable the ransom should be God to find, as the interpreting angel had been God to provide, so that what saves the man is not his own righteousness but a ransom found for him, and observes that such words must have fallen on Job ear gratefully, confirming his old longing for a daysman; on the restoration he will not choose between the two senses, finding the passage a description of the restoration of a penitent and of a recovery from sickness at once, and he prefers the reading that makes the following verse the man own confession, that he had sinned and perverted what was right and it was not requited to him; Keil and Delitzsch give the whole of it in their rendering, down to the singing to men and the soul delivered from the pit.

debates.question: Who is the messenger, the interpreter, one among a thousand?

sides.position: not a created angel but a minister of the word, an interpreter of the Scriptures, and such a man is rare
a prophet or teacher qualified to expound the providence and point out the design of God in it
a remarkable anticipation of the office of the Advocate with the Father, and an indication of the mediation of the Son
an angel acting as mediator, one of a thousand, to declare to man what is for his profit

debates.question: Is the restoration of the flesh bodily or spiritual?

sides.position: bodily, and comparative only, the man who was skin and bone becoming plump and ruddy again
spiritual throughout, the man born a new creature and returning to the days of his youth as a child of God
both at once, the restoration of a penitent and the recovery of a sick man described together

outliers: Ellicott alone makes a point of the ransom being God to find rather than man to offer, and joins it to the angel being God to provide.
Clarke alone reads every clause of the recovery as regeneration rather than returning health.
themes: an interpreter at a sick bed
a ransom God found himself
flesh fresher than a child
a confession sung before men

29.pericope_label: Lo, all these things worketh God oftentimes with man, to bring back his soul from the pit and to be enlightened with the light of the living; mark well, O Job, hearken unto me, and if thou hast anything to say answer me, for I desire to justify thee

schools.summary: Gill takes the verse as an express summary, that God is an operating being always at work in providence, sometimes on men minds in dreams, sometimes by affliction, sometimes by his ministers, and notes that the word rendered oftentimes is in the original twice, so that when once will not serve he repeats it; on the closing charge he reads it as an instruction to weigh what has been said and attend to what is still to come.

Henry lists the instruments in the same way, conscience and providences and ministers and mercies and afflictions, with God making men sick and making them well again, trying another affliction when one has not done the work and a mercy when neither has, and sending a messenger to interpret both; he marks the difference between the two methods already described, that the dream was to keep the soul back from the pit, which is to prevent sin, while sickness and the word are to bring the soul back, which is to recover those who have fallen into it; he closes the summary devotionally, asking what man is that God should thus visit him, and draws two consequences, that we should comply with God designs and work with him for our own good rather than counter-work him, and that those who perish will be left inexcusable, since so much was done to save them and they would not be healed; and he sets the desire to justify Job against the other friends, who wished to condemn where this one wishes to justify, making a rule of it, that those we reprove we should also wish to see clear themselves.

Clarke makes the numeral three times over, or, since the form is dual, twice three times, which he takes for again and again, and breaks off to bless God for it; he reads the invitation to answer as sincere, since it is the speaker desire that Job should stand clear of all charges, and ends with the manuscripts, reporting that one authority reads according to his righteousness for his righteousness, and that many manuscripts, early editions and versions give my soul and my life where the received text has his, which would turn the close of the passage into the man own words; Wesley quotes Henry passage on the inexcusable, names him as its author and calls the words excellent, and then turns on the second consequence with four questions, how much did God do to save them, did he ever do anything to save them, did he ever design to save them, and if not, how can what was never done nor even designed leave them inexcusable, letting the objection stand unanswered.

Ellicott calls the verse the very key-note of Elihu doctrine, that the dealings of God are for education and discipline, and that this is what he wishes to impress on Job, and he explains what the justifying would amount to, that Job is to be vindicated before his friends by the argument that his afflictions came not for past sin but as a preservative against a possible future defection, on which ground his case may honestly be defended; Keil and Delitzsch render the four closing verses plainly, the bringing back of the soul from the pit, the charge to listen and be silent, the invitation to answer, and the promise of wisdom if there is no answer.

debates.question: Does so much having been done to save men leave those who perish inexcusable?

sides.position: yes; so much was done to save them and they would not be healed, which should engage us to comply with God designs rather than counter-work him
the words are excellent but the inference will not stand: how much was done, was anything done, was anything even designed, and if not, how can what was never designed leave a man inexcusable

debates.question: What does the speaker mean by desiring to justify Job?

sides.position: that Job be vindicated before his friends, his afflictions being not for past sin but a preservative against a possible future defection
that he contends for truth and not for victory, unlike the three who wished to condemn
that Job should stand clear of all charges, which is why the invitation to answer is sincere

outliers: Wesley alone quotes another commentator in this collection by name, praises the passage and then disputes its conclusion, leaving the objection open.
Clarke alone closes with a list of manuscript variants which would turn the end of the passage into the restored man own speech.
themes: a summary of all the methods
twice and thrice with one man
a dispute recorded between two commentators
a reprover who wants the man acquitted
